title: Dissertation - Case Studies
section: The Modality Effect: Investigating Differential Memory Encoding for Visual and Auditory Stimuli
text:
The Modality Effect: Investigating Differential Memory Encoding for Visual and Auditory Stimuli
Technologies & Platforms Used: Gorilla.sc

How do our brains prioritize information based on how it is delivered? In this research project, we investigated the influence of sensory modality on the encoding of neutral verbal stimuli. By utilizing Gorilla.sc, we developed a rigorous online experiment that isolated visual and auditory presentation methods, requiring participants to perform a recognition task following initial exposure. This project highlights the critical role of technical support in psychological research, with the Psychology Technical team providing end-to-end guidance in experimental development, stimulus control, and the technical orchestration of the study’s logical flow.

title: Dissertation - Case Studies
section: “Do We Know What We Know? Examining Confidence and Capacity in Episodic Memory”
text:
“Do We Know What We Know? Examining Confidence and Capacity in Episodic Memory”
Technologies & Platforms Used: Gorilla.sc

A key question in cognitive aging and psychology is how well our confidence in our memory—our self-efficacy—aligns with our actual performance. In this project, we leveraged the Gorilla.sc platform to deploy a two-part assessment. First, participants completed the MIA-Revised Capacity scale to gauge their perceived memory capabilities. Following this, they performed a series of episodic memory tasks involving the identification of neutral, everyday stimuli. This study served as a critical exploration of whether high memory self-efficacy translates to superior mnemonic accuracy.

title: Dissertation - Case Studies
section: Where Does the Magic Happen? An Eye-Tracking Analysis of Misdirection
text:
Where Does the Magic Happen? An Eye-Tracking Analysis of Misdirection
Technologies & Platforms Used: Tobii EyeTracking, Gorilla.sc, Tobii Pro Labs

Magic is fundamentally a study of human attention. In this dissertation project, we collaborated with a Wrexham University colleague to deconstruct the art of the ‘classic sleight.’ The student asked a critical question: when witnessing a magic trick, do we follow the eyes or the hands? By tracking the visual gaze of participants as they observed a live magic routine, this research mapped the precise moments where human attention is captured, held, and—ultimately—misdirected.

title: Psychometric Scales Repository
text:
Psychologists regularly use psychometric scales to collect data about peoples attitudes, personality, perceptions, or behaviour (amongst other things).
The questionnaires, scales, and inventories listed below are a great place to get started on looking for a suitable measure for your research. Although, there are many measures that are listed below. You may find a more suitable measure by conducting a Library Search, using Google Scholar, or by other means. If you come across something interesting that you think we should look at, please let us know!



We do not have copyright authority over some measures and cannot grant permission for use.
We recommend students from Wrexham University to use the “Free for use” scales. If you require a particular scale, then please contact the author(s) of the questionnaire for use permissions. However, please consult your supervisor before proceeding.
The scales are provided solely as a courtesy to help Dissertation students develop their experiments efficiently, to get their projects underway, and provide module leaders resources for their teaching modules. Not all scales are provided and will only be available when Wrexham students, researchers and module leaders provide the appropriate evidence of licensing or permission.
Please note that the scales may contain errors. Therefore, if you identify any inaccuracies, please kindly contact us at psychology.technician@wrexham.ac.uk so we can rectify any of the scales. While every effort has been made to ensure accuracy, these materials are prepared by humans and should be carefully checked before use in any research or teaching capacity.
Additionally, it is the responsibility of each researcher to ensure the information they use from this repository is accurate and complies with copyright law. Some scales will also dictate that you cannot modify or adapt the contents of the scale, so if you should use a scale from this repository it should follow the appropriate copyright licensing from the original publishers. For more information about copyright and how it applies to research materials, please see the UK Government’s guidance on copyright: https://www.gov.uk/copyright.
Please note: Due to the volume of requests, emails requesting permission for use will not receive a reply. We are also unable to provide author contact information.
If you have further questions, you can contact: psychology.technician@wrexham.ac.uk

section: Essential Checklist for Choosing & Using Psychometric Scales
text:
Essential Checklist for Choosing & Using Psychometric Scales
What we can provide with assistance is some helpful pointers when searching for your Psychometric scale. So firstly, before selecting a psychometric scale or questionnaire for your research project, work through these key considerations to ensure your measure is both scientifically valid and ethically sound:

Licensing & Terms of Use: Verify whether the scale is freely available in the public domain or requires explicit permission/payment from the copyright holder before distribution.
Ethical Approval: Ensure the content of the scale is age-appropriate, non-triggering for your target demographic, and explicitly approved by your ethics committee. If you do use sensitive scales then make sure you provide information on mitigation factors via a Risk assessment or appropriate information in your Particiapant information sheet and online ethics application for using that scale.
Item Redundancy & Subscales: Check if the scale contains overlapping or redundant items. Group questions into their correct underlying subscale dimensions prior to analysis.
Scoring & Aggregation Rules: Review the author’s scoring manual to determine whether to sum or average item responses, handle reverse-scored items, and manage missing data points.

section: Key Concepts to Keep in Mind
text:
Key Concepts to Keep in Mind

Reverse Scoring: Identify negative or oppositely phrased items (e.g., “I rarely feel happy” on a self-esteem scale) and invert their values before calculating subscale totals.
Calculating Subscale Scores: Compute separate composite scores (mean or sum) for each distinct subscale rather than collapsing everything into a single overall score, unless the original validation paper explicitly supports doing so.
Item Redundancy: Look out for questions that ask virtually the same thing in slightly different ways. Highly redundant items inflate internal consistency (\(\alpha\)) artificially without adding genuine psychological information.

title: Using Gorilla.sc for your Dissertation Project
text:
Phase 1: Task Design & Logic (Task Builder)
Trial Structure & Canvas Layout

Set up explicit fixations/crosses with clear display durations (e.g., 500 ms).
Ensure response buttons or keypresses are bound to explicit zones.
Define explicit screen bounds and scaling so elements render cleanly across varying monitor sizes.

Stimulus Management

Upload stimulus files (images, audio, video) using consistent, clear file names.



Verify media preload settings (e.g., set critical visual or audio stimuli to preload before trial display to prevent timing lag).

Spreadsheet Construction

Map columns directly to task zones (e.g., stimulus_image, correct_response).



Add a randomise_blocks or randomise_trials column to control trial sequence per participant.
Specify a display column to direct Gorilla which screen layout to call for each row.

Data & Metric Logging

Check that Reaction Time (RT), accuracy logging are toggled ON for response screens.
Check that psychometric measures are obtaining appropriate values and follow the exact formatting



Set up correct key bindings and response tags (e.g., space = target, f/j = binary choice).


Phase 2: Experiment Flow & Logic (Experiment Tree)

Participant Routing

Include an Participant Information & Informed Consent screen at the very beginning.
Add a Demographics Questionnaire (or screening checks) prior to the core task.
Place Instructions nodes with brief comprehension checks before major tasks.

Randomization & Counterbalancing

Use Randomiser nodes to assign participants to conditions or task orders evenly.
Use Branching nodes to divert participants based on accuracy, demographics, or consent answers.

Data Quality & Rejection Controls

Add an Attention Check or Catch Trial node to screen out low-effort responses.
Set up a Branching / Reject path for participants who fail attention checks or decline consent.

Recruitment Platform Integration

Place a Redirect / Finish node at the end with appropriate completion URLs (e.g., Prolific, CloudResearch, or Qualtrics parameters).
Pass participant query parameters (PROLIFIC_PID, STUDY_ID, SESSION_ID) into Gorilla embedded variables.




Phase 3: Pilot Testing & Data Audit

Technical Validation

Test the experiment link in Preview Mode across multiple browser types (Chrome, Safari, Firefox).
Check the task on both desktop and mobile layouts (or set device restrictions in the Experiment Tree settings).




Data Export Verification

Run a full mock session and export the Data CSV.
Confirm that key columns (Response, Reaction Time, Spreadsheet Row, Correct, Participant ID) are present and accurate.
Verify that spreadsheet values parse cleanly without missing data or mismatched headers.




Phase 4: Launching your Experiment
As previously mentioned, once you are ready to launch your study then follow this link here for a full guide to make sure you have followed everything: https://support.gorilla.sc/support/launching-your-study/index
We have inserted the guide above so you can get the full information above. However, when you are indeed ready to launch your experiment then please watch this video set by gorilla.sc: https://support.gorilla.sc/support/launching-your-study/create-to-launch#launchyourexperiment
Finally, once you have requested the Tokens the Psychology Technicians will accept your token requests and then you will have to accept the tokens by requesting that same number again. It’s a little bit confusing I know but this is how Gorilla.sc is set up!

title: Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)
text:
Not sure what we do? We’ve put together this guide to answer common questions and help you navigate our services. Whether you’re a student or a new staff member, you’ll find everything you need to know about our technical support right here.


What kind of technical support do you provide?

We provide support for hardware setup, lab equipment access, and platform troubleshooting (e.g., JISC/Gorilla). Please note that we do not provide academic tutoring, proofreading, or feedback on your research design or academic writing.



How do I access JISC?

Please contact psychology.technicians@wrexham.ac.uk and request an account on JISC for the specific module. Please CC your supervisor / module leader for the JISC when sending the email.



How do I access Gorilla.sc?

Please contact psychology.technicians@wrexham.ac.uk and request an account on Gorilla.sc for the specific module. Please CC your supervisor / module leader for the Gorilla.sc when sending the email.



Where can I get access for support from the technicians for my dissertation project?

For technical support regarding your dissertation—such as equipment booking, software setup, or lab space access—please submit a request via the PsychTech Booking System.



Can you please help me with my data analysis?

We cannot help in analysing your dissertation/module related data. We can only provide demonstrations and cannot guide your analysis process. Please refer to the appropriate research methods modules for selecting the appropriate models and analysis for appropriate guidance.



I need to book a session on the day, please can you help?

To ensure we can provide the best possible support, we kindly ask that all bookings are made at least 24 hours in advance. This lead time allows our team to plan our daily schedule effectively, as we are often focused on specialised tasks and are not always able to monitor the booking inbox in real-time.



What do I do if equipment is damaged or malfunctioning?

Please report any issues immediately to the Psychology Technician team at psychology.technicians@wrexham.ac.uk. Please include a photo of the damage and the asset tag number if available. Do not attempt to repair equipment yourself; we are here to handle all maintenance.



How do I install this application on my personal computer?

We provide support for software used within the university labs. For installations on personal devices, please visit the Wrexham IT Support Portal Link for university-licensed software availability. We are unable to provide technical support for personal hardware or non-university software.



 I’m having trouble connecting to the university Wi-Fi in the lab/campus. Can the Psychology Technicians help?

As the Psychology Technician team, we focus on research-specific software and equipment. We do not have access to the university’s core network infrastructure or student Wi-Fi credentials.



Where can I find resources for statistics?

Although we cannot provide help with statistics directly and you are looking for specific statistics or data analysis resources beyond what is provided by the university course then do book a Initial Discussion meeting via the Booking System.



 Does my research need a Risk Assessment?

Yes. All experiments conducted within Wrexham University require a completed Risk Assessment as a mandatory component of your Ethics submission. This process ensures the safety of both the researcher and your participants. You do not need to navigate this process alone. For guidance on identifying hazards and implementing safety protocols, please consult:

Your Research Supervisor: They provide oversight for project-specific risks and ethical requirements.
The Psychology Technician Team: We are available to support the technical aspects of your assessment, including lab safety protocols, equipment handling, and experimental environment configurations.




Can you help with my data cleaning

We can guide you through the data cleaning procedure to an extent, we will not be directly manipulating the dataset itself, but assistance with the data cleaning is only minimal.



 Can you help me in setting up my experiment?

We provide full support on experiments if requested by the student and your supervisor of your dissertation project. This means that if you get stuck along the way with creating your experiment then we can directly help by fixing any derailment during the creation of your study.



 I have a very niche and technical idea I want to do, can you help?

We recommend you discuss with us or your supervisor if you want to conduct any technical ideas that you wish to conduct for your dissertation project. You can also setup a Initial Discussion meeting via the Booking System for this purpose!


If there’s a question that doesn’t appear here that you need to find out then please do send an email to psychology.technician@Wrexham.ac.uk and we will respond to your query within 4 working days.

Plan to use digital, rather than paper, forms and stimuli if possible.
Reduce the number of devices used simultaneously.
Investigate if you can make use of unused equipment or share resources across projects.
Group data collection sessions to reduce setup frequency.

Below is a selection of recommended resources that are freely available to students and staff. We describe as well how we as the psychology technicians use these tools down below to help our students.




Questionnaire Page
Experimental Page






Quarto A publishing system for creating reproducible documents, dashboards, and interactive reports. Useful for writing, data analysis, and creating professional portfolios. We use this to output a plethora of content for students.
Open Reproducibility Resources
A growing repository and set of tools that ensure transparency in research, demonstrations and teaching materials. Primarily on Gorilla.sc Open Materials.






Python A versatile language for data analysis, statistics, machine learning, and experiment design. Widely supported across psychology and cognitive science research.
R A powerful statistical environment for quantitative analysis, data visualization, and reproducible research.
Julia A high-performance programming language particularly suited for numerical computing, data analysis, and modelling. Widely used in research requiring speed and scalability, and increasingly adopted in psychology and cognitive science applications.






Open Broadcaster Software A free and open source software for video recording and live streaming.
DaVinci Resolve A professional-grade video editing suite with a free version. Suitable for creating teaching material, experiment stimuli, or presentation content.
Audacity An open-source audio editing tool, useful for preparing stimuli and cleaning recordings.
GIMP / Inkscape Free alternatives to Photoshop and Illustrator, excellent for creating figures, posters, and experimental graphics.

Unity Experimental Framework – A flexible platform for creating interactive VR experiments and simulations.
Unity & Unity Hub – Centralized management for Unity projects, versions, and collaboration.
Unreal Engine – High-fidelity engine for immersive VR environments and realistic experimental scenarios.
Blender – 3D modelling and animation software to design custom stimuli and experimental assets.

title: Counselling Research Ethics Guidance for Students
text:
Document status and authorship — This page has been generated collaboratively using artificial intelligence and human academic oversight. It is not a final or static policy document. It is a living, evolving resource intended to support Counselling students across academic years in understanding and applying research ethics in practice. It should be read alongside formal university ethics procedures, your professional body’s code, and supervisor guidance. Students are encouraged to consult only the sections relevant to their specific project rather than reading the document in its entirety; however, those intending to practise as counsellors or psychotherapists are strongly advised to engage with the full document, as the ethical reasoning it describes is the same reasoning you will use in clinical practice.
Do / Do Not Guidance:

✅ Use this document as a practical guide alongside formal procedures
✅ Read only the sections that are directly relevant to your specific project
❌ Treat this as a final or exhaustive policy
❌ Feel obliged to read every section if it is not relevant to your study



Counselling in the UK is not governed by a single statutory regulator. Instead, practitioners belong to professional bodies that hold Accredited Registers overseen by the Professional Standards Authority. The two most relevant to Wrexham Counselling students are:

BACP — British Association for Counselling and Psychotherapy: Ethical Framework for the Counselling Professions
NCPS — National Counselling and Psychotherapy Society: Code of Ethics

For research specifically, BACP publishes a dedicated companion document that the Ethical Framework requires members to follow:

Ethical Guidelines for Research in the Counselling Professions (BACP, last updated February 2019)

NCPS embeds its research requirements directly within the Code of Ethics, in the Research Ethics section.






ImportantThe BACP Ethical Framework is changing



BACP launched a new Ethical Framework for the Counselling Professions 2026, which becomes mandatory at midday on Tuesday 3 November 2026. Until then, the 2018 framework remains the operative document.
The 2026 framework restructures into three sections — working ethically within relationships, ethical principles, and core responsibilities — and adds new guidance on the use of AI and digital technology. It also asks members to articulate a rationale for their ethical decision-making, which is directly relevant to how you justify design choices in an ethics application.
If you are writing a dissertation that will be submitted after November 2026, cite the 2026 framework. If your project concludes before then, cite 2018. Check with your supervisor which applies to your submission date.


A note on which body applies to you. If you are a student member of BACP or NCPS, you are bound by that body’s code now, as a student, not only after qualifying. If you are a member of neither, your project is still governed by Wrexham’s REC and by whichever framework your programme aligns to. Ask your supervisor if you are unsure — the answer changes what you cite in your application.




This document supports Counselling students in preparing ethically sound research proposals and ethics applications. Its aim is to translate the ethical commitments of the counselling professions into practical guidance that aligns with the expectations of Research Ethics Committees (RECs). The emphasis throughout is on ethical viability, feasibility, and institutional responsibility, rather than simply regulatory compliance.
It provides guidance on:

practical implementation of BACP and NCPS ethics in a research context,
common pitfalls for student researchers,
additional considerations for REC review,
the particular hazards of researching as a trainee practitioner,
and guidance for managing sensitive or complex aspects of research.

Do / Do Not Guidance:

✅ Consult supervisors early and regularly
✅ Consider practical feasibility as well as ethical principles
❌ Assume mere adherence to rules ensures ethical approval
❌ Start data collection without REC approval





Both frameworks share a common ancestry in principle-based ethics, so they overlap substantially. Where they differ is in emphasis and structure: BACP separates values, principles and personal moral qualities, while NCPS sets out five fundamental principles drawing explicitly on Kitchener (1984) and Kitchener and Anderson (2011).


The 2018 Ethical Framework has three main parts: Our commitment to clients, Ethics, and Good practice. The Ethics section is the one you will most often cite in a research rationale.
BACP core principles:







Principle
Meaning




Being trustworthy
Honouring the trust placed in the practitioner


Autonomy
Respect for the client’s right to be self-governing


Beneficence
A commitment to promoting the client’s wellbeing


Non-maleficence
A commitment to avoiding harm to the client


Justice
Fair and impartial treatment of all clients; adequate provision of services


Self-respect
Fostering the practitioner’s self-knowledge, integrity and care for self



BACP is explicit that these principles will sometimes conflict, and that a decision is not unethical merely because it is controversial or because another practitioner would have decided differently. What is required is that you consider all relevant circumstances with care and remain accountable for the decision you made. This is precisely the reasoning an REC wants to see in an application — not a claim that your study is risk-free, but a demonstration that you identified the tensions and reasoned through them.
BACP also names personal moral qualities that practitioners aspire to, several of which bear directly on research conduct: candour, courage, diligence, humility, integrity, resilience and wisdom.




Working towards the good of clients and doing no harm (Beneficence and Non-maleficence) — practitioners hold client welfare central and commit to avoiding harm.
Being trustworthy and responsible (Fidelity) — honouring trust placed by clients and the community, and representing the profession respectfully.
Respect for the dignity and rights of the client (Autonomy) — the right to self-determination, with Gillick competence and the Fraser Guidelines considered where applicable.
Justice — awareness of one’s own judgements and prejudices, using supervision as a safeguard, and respect for diversity of persons.
Integrity and self-responsibility — honesty and accuracy, alongside responsibility for one’s own health, wellbeing and scope of competence.

NCPS states that these principles cannot deliver a single “right” answer, but can be used to reach a best clinical judgement — and that a practitioner must be able to demonstrate they considered them, especially in discussion with their supervisor.

If your project sits under one body, cite that body. If your cohort spans both, citing the shared principle and noting both sources is acceptable and often clearer.
Do / Do Not Guidance:

✅ Cite the framework your professional membership actually binds you to
✅ Show your reasoning where principles pull against each other
❌ Cite the BPS Code of Human Research Ethics as your governing framework — it governs psychologists, not counsellors
❌ Treat the principles as a checklist to be ticked rather than a reasoning structure








The Ethical Framework sets out research obligations in its Good practice section. In summary, BACP members undertaking research commit to being rigorously attentive to the quality and integrity of the research process, the knowledge claims arising from it, and how results are disseminated. All research must be guided by the Ethical Guidelines for Research in the Counselling Professions, all participants must take part on the basis of explicit informed consent, and all research must be reviewed in advance so that participants’ rights and interests are considered independently of the researcher. Research methods must comply with good practice standards for any services being delivered and must not adversely affect clients.
That independent-review requirement is why REC approval is not a bureaucratic formality — it is the mechanism by which the framework’s own standard is met.
The Ethical Guidelines for Research are organised into twelve sections, several of which are directly relevant to dissertation projects:

Ethical principles and research
Research integrity
Safety and managing the risks of research to participants, the public and the researcher
Relationships and communication with research participants
Vulnerability in research participants
Research ethics review and research governance
Online research
Trainee and student researchers
Ethical problem-solving in research

Section 9 is written for you specifically. Read it before drafting your application.



The NCPS Code of Ethics contains a Research Ethics section stating that where research directly involves clients or trainees, all clauses of the Code apply. In addition, researchers must:

Accept that participation is purely voluntary, with no pressure of any type exerted. Payment must not act as an inducement where the research asks participants to take risks beyond those of everyday life.
Obtain proper consent before commencement, especially with minors or persons with special needs. In longitudinal research, consent may need to be repeated at intervals.
Make clear at the outset that initial consent does not negate the right to withdraw at any stage.
Maintain complete openness and honesty about the purpose and nature of the research.
Consider potential adverse consequences and be ready to signpost to support.
Inform a participant if, during research, they present a condition they seem unaware of — and advise them if continued participation may jeopardise their future wellbeing.
Provide for the ongoing care of participants regarding adverse effects arising within a reasonable period after involvement.
Act on the principle that the privacy and psychological wellbeing of the individual participant is always more important than the research itself.

Point 8 is the one to internalise. It is the sentence to return to whenever a design decision trades participant welfare against data quality.






NoteNote on the incentive clause



NCPS permits payment but forbids it as an inducement to accept risk. A modest thank-you (a prize draw entry, a voucher) is generally acceptable; a payment large enough to make a participant tolerate distress they would otherwise avoid is not. Explain your reasoning in the application rather than simply stating the amount.


Do / Do Not Guidance:

✅ Read BACP’s Ethical Guidelines for Research, section 9, if you are a BACP member
✅ Read the NCPS Code’s Research Ethics section if you are an NCPS member
✅ Plan for after-the-fact support, not just in-the-moment debriefing
❌ Assume the Code applies only to clinical work and not to your dissertation
❌ Set an incentive level without justifying it






This section has no equivalent in psychology-oriented ethics guidance, and it is the single most common reason counselling dissertation proposals require substantial revision.
As a counselling student you occupy two roles at once: trainee practitioner and student researcher. These roles carry different obligations, different relationships to the people in front of you, and different kinds of power. Confusing them causes real harm.


You must not recruit your own current clients as research participants. The reasons are cumulative and each would be sufficient on its own:

Consent cannot be freely given. A client depends on you therapeutically. “No” is much harder to say to your counsellor than to a stranger with a clipboard.
The therapeutic frame is compromised. Material disclosed in therapy is disclosed for therapeutic purposes. Repurposing it as data breaches the basis on which it was shared.
Dual relationship. BACP requires that dual or multiple relationships be avoided where the risks of harm to the client outweigh the benefits. Researcher-and-therapist is a textbook example.
Withdrawal becomes unsafe. A participant who withdraws mid-study must be able to continue therapy unaffected — and neither of you can be confident that is true.

Former clients are only marginally less problematic, and any such proposal needs explicit supervisory and REC discussion before it is drafted.



Recruiting other clients from your placement agency is sometimes possible but is never straightforward. It requires:

Gatekeeper permission from the agency, in writing, independent of your own placement relationship
Recruitment that does not run through you as their counsellor or a colleague with therapeutic contact
Clear communication that participation has no bearing whatsoever on the service they receive
A plan for what happens if a participant discloses something about the service, a colleague, or their own risk

Many agencies will decline, and they are entitled to. Build your timeline assuming a “no” is possible, and have an alternative population identified before you submit.



Counselling students are, by training, good at opening people up. That skill becomes an ethical hazard in a research interview, where you have no therapeutic contract, no ongoing relationship, and no mandate to work with what emerges.
The distinction to hold onto: you use counselling skills to conduct a humane interview, but you are not offering therapy. You listen well, you notice distress, you respond with warmth — and then you signpost rather than intervene.
Do / Do Not Guidance:

✅ Use counselling skills to make the interview safe, paced and respectful
✅ Pause, offer a break, or end the interview if a participant becomes distressed
✅ Have a written signposting list ready before the first interview
✅ Take the emotional impact of interviews to research supervision
❌ Follow distressing material deeper because it is producing rich data
❌ Offer interpretations, reframes, or therapeutic homework
❌ Slide into a therapeutic contract mid-interview
❌ Research your own current clients under any framing




Clinical supervision and research supervision are different, and you will likely have both. Clinical supervision addresses your practice with clients; research supervision addresses your project. Material from research participants should go to your research supervisor, within the confidentiality terms your participants agreed to — not into clinical supervision, where participants never consented for it to go.
If a research interview has affected you personally, that is appropriate for clinical supervision or personal therapy, discussed at the level of your own reaction rather than the participant’s disclosures.





Do / Do Not Guidance:

✅ Provide clear rationale, methodology, and risk management plans
✅ Demonstrate researcher competence and supervision arrangements
✅ State explicitly how you have separated practitioner and researcher roles
❌ Submit vague or incomplete proposals
❌ Assume feasibility without evidence

Key areas of REC evaluation include:

Feasibility within the academic timeframe
Appropriateness of the sample and recruitment method
Data protection, storage, and UK GDPR compliance
Researcher competence and supervision
Institutional risk and liability
Management of dual roles and power imbalance
Adequacy of distress protocols and signposting
Researcher safety and wellbeing







Do / Do Not Guidance:

✅ Use scales free for research or educational purposes
✅ Frame measures as assessing traits, experiences, or self-reported states
✅ Check licensing terms in writing before building your survey
❌ Use copyrighted or proprietary measures without permission
❌ Attempt to diagnose or imply clinical assessment

Note that widely used outcome measures in counselling (for example the CORE family of measures) have their own licensing and usage conditions. Confirm terms before you design around them.



Do / Do Not Guidance:

✅ Use university-approved, UK GDPR-compliant platforms
✅ Store data within institutional systems
❌ Use unapproved third-party platforms (e.g., Google Forms)
❌ Store participant data on personal or external cloud services

NCPS makes the same point for practice: only use platforms that are secure in terms of GDPR, confidentiality, hacking and data storage, and follow ICO guidance. The Society explicitly declines to endorse or forbid specific platforms because the market changes too quickly — which means the responsibility for checking sits with you and your institution.



Do / Do Not Guidance:

✅ Conduct research in approved university facilities
✅ Book rooms, equipment, and risk assessments in advance
✅ Consult the technical team about room and equipment requirements at psychology-technician@wrexham.ac.uk
❌ Conduct research in unapproved or unsafe locations
❌ Ignore risk assessment procedures
❌ Conduct interviews in a participant’s home without a lone-working protocol




BACP’s research guidelines treat researcher safety as an ethical requirement in its own right, not an afterthought — and both frameworks name practitioner wellbeing as a principle (BACP’s self-respect; NCPS’s integrity and self-responsibility).
Qualitative counselling research means sustained exposure to difficult material. This has a cumulative effect that students routinely underestimate.
Do / Do Not Guidance:

✅ Agree a lone-working protocol before any off-campus data collection
✅ Space interviews out rather than clustering them
✅ Build transcription time into your plan — you will hear the material again
✅ Use supervision for the impact the work has on you
❌ Schedule six emotionally demanding interviews in a week to save time
❌ Treat your own distress as a private problem separate from the project




Do / Do Not Guidance:

✅ Avoid deception unless genuinely necessary
✅ Fully debrief participants if deception is used
❌ Mislead participants unnecessarily
❌ Leave participants unaware of study purpose

Note that NCPS requires “complete openness and honesty with regard to both the purpose and nature of the research”. Deception designs are therefore a harder sell in counselling research than in experimental psychology, and need strong justification.



No project may investigate, trial, evaluate, or in any way facilitate practices intended to change or suppress sexual orientation or gender identity. You must demonstrate that you have anticipated potential emotional, psychological, or social risks and put appropriate safeguards in place. Ethical viability depends not only on what is studied, but how. Question wording, task framing, sequencing of measures, and the context of participation all influence participant wellbeing. ✅ Provide a clear theoretical and empirical justification for studying the sensitive topic
✅ Demonstrate proportionality between research aims and participant burden
✅ Include content warnings and remind participants of their right to skip questions
✅ Implement robust debriefing and signposting procedures
✅ Write a distress protocol specifying what you will do, at what threshold
✅ Consult supervisors early and revise designs where risk is disproportionate
❌ Include sensitive questions without strong justification
❌ Use graphic, explicit, or unnecessarily detailed materials
❌ Assume participants will not experience distress
❌ Proceed without clear plans for managing adverse reactions

✅ Use non-diagnostic, research-appropriate self-report measures
✅ State clearly that measures do not provide clinical assessment or diagnosis

✅ Include tailored support and wellbeing signposting in debrief materials

Use the university templates linked above

Decide upon your research question

Decide the method: interview, focus group, observation

✅ Keep records adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary
✅ Store data on institutional systems, encrypted, with access limited to the research team
✅ Agree a retention and destruction schedule and state it to participants
✅ Transport any physical materials in a locked container
❌ Keep recordings on a phone or personal laptop
❌ Promise absolute confidentiality — you cannot deliver it
❌ Discuss identifiable participant material in open forums or group chats

✅ Engage supervisors and technical staff early
✅ Prepare ethical applications with clarity and feasibility in mind
✅ Read the research guidance for your own professional body, not just this page
✅ Use the Wrexham Research Ethics Student Guide (WRIS: undergraduate, postgraduate)

❌ Assume mere adherence to rules ensures ethical approval
❌ Start data collection without REC approval

title: Psychology Research Ethics Guidance for Students
text:
This guidance is grounded in the British Psychological Society (BPS) Code of Human Research Ethics: https://www.bps.org.uk/guideline/bps-code-human-research-ethics
The BPS framework emphasises practical values that must be operationalised in all psychology research. Additional ethical considerations incorporated here include confidentiality, researcher-participant boundaries, demographic justification, incentives, and environmental/social responsibility.


Researchers must recognise participants as autonomous agents with the right to make informed, voluntary decisions about participation.
Do / Do Not Guidance:

✅ Provide clear, accessible information and consent procedures
✅ Respect participant autonomy and withdrawal rights
❌ Coerce or mislead participants
❌ Deny or obscure withdrawal options




Research must be methodologically sound, theoretically justified, and conducted with honesty and transparency.
Do / Do Not Guidance:

✅ Use validated, appropriate methods
✅ Justify all methodological choices
❌ Conduct research without planning or justification
❌ Fabricate or misrepresent data or methods




Researchers must consider broader social, institutional, and cultural consequences of their work, including cultural sensitivity, inclusivity, and environmental/institutional risks.
Do / Do Not Guidance:

✅ Protect vulnerable groups and consider societal impacts
✅ Address potential misuses of findings
✅ Ensure cultural and demographic considerations are justified
✅ Mitigate environmental or institutional risks
❌ Conduct research likely to harm or stigmatise participants
❌ Ignore wider implications of findings




All research involves some level of risk. Ethical research requires these risks to be proportionate, justified, and actively mitigated.
Do / Do Not Guidance:

✅ Assess and mitigate risks
✅ Provide debriefing and support mechanisms
❌ Expose participants to unnecessary harm
❌ Assume participants can manage distress without support




Researchers must ensure participant data is kept confidential and anonymised wherever possible.
Do / Do Not Guidance:

✅ Anonymise or pseudonymise participant data
✅ Explain limits of confidentiality in consent forms
❌ Share identifiable data without explicit consent
❌ Store sensitive data on personal devices without institutional approval




Researchers must maintain professional boundaries and minimise power imbalances.
Do / Do Not Guidance:

✅ Maintain professional relationships and boundaries
✅ Avoid implicit pressure due to authority or institutional roles
❌ Exploit relationships or position of power
❌ Coerce participation through hierarchical pressure




Demographic questions must be justified and referenced. Only collect what is necessary for research objectives.
Do / Do Not Guidance:

✅ Collect only necessary demographic information
✅ Provide references for why each demographic variable is needed
❌ Collect all demographics without justification
❌ Include sensitive demographics without rationale




Use of incentives must not coerce participation. Participants can withdraw without losing rewards.
Do / Do Not Guidance:

✅ Explain incentives and withdrawal rights
✅ Ensure rewards are proportionate and ethical
❌ Use incentives to pressure participation
❌ Link participation to rewards in a way that creates undue influence

Do / Do Not Guidance:

✅ Engage supervisors and technical staff early
✅ Prepare ethical applications with clarity and feasibility in mind
✅ Read the research guidance for your own professional body, not just this page
✅ Use the Wrexham Research Ethics Student Guide (WRIS: undergraduate, postgraduate)

text:
2-1-Research Aims
Provide your research aims and objectives of your dissertation project.

In this section, clearly state what your dissertation project intends to achieve. Your aim should give an overall statement of the purpose of your study, while your objectives should break this down into specific, achievable steps. These must align with your research question and the methods you intend to use.

Please provide details of your research design (Please use lay language free from technical terms) 

Next, briefly outline how you plan to conduct your research. This may include your methodology (e.g., experimental, survey, qualitative interviews), sampling approach, data‑collection techniques, and any key procedures. Keep this section concise but clear enough for reviewers to understand your planned process. Your reviewer will not be from the Psychology department, so try to avoid using any technical terms from the psychological sciences.

Describe the potential benefits and impacts of your research, this can involve improving our current knowledge of the literature, how to improve a service etc.

Here, explain how your research may be valuable. Potential benefits might include:

Contributing to or updating existing psychological literature
Highlighting gaps in current knowledge (I would avoid saying research gaps)
Informing practice or improving a service
Providing insights that could guide future research or interventions


You do not need to guarantee outcomes—simply outline the possible positive contributions your work may offer.

Examples:

LinkedIn Groups (Unless they have a post saying they are open to posts, however you must supply in the ethics application evidence of this via screenshot)
Facebook Groups
Reddit Forums
External Communities


Gatekeeper approval is not normally required when recruiting via:

Open university-approved recruitment systems (e.g. PsychTech Moodle Page, Student Intranet)
Your own personal social media without targeting a specific group
Fully open public spaces where no permission is required and no moderation exists

Evidence - Later you will need to show this evidence of approval/permission by the gatekeeper. This can be:

Email or written confirmation from a gatekeeper or administrator
A screenshot of group rules explicitly allowing research recruitment
A message confirming permission to post recruitment materials

Common Mistakes - Some pitfalls to avoid so you don’t get rejected in your application process.

Assuming “public” means “permission not needed”
Posting without moderator approval
Failing to upload screenshots or written evidence
Treating online communities differently from physical organisations

If in doubt, assume approval is required and seek clarification. Please also speak with your supervisor, as some organisations are classed as higher‑risk (i.e. NHS, Schools, Prisons) for ethical review. These may require additional scrutiny, longer approval times, or further documentation before your application can be approved. Essentially, if someone controls access to your pool of participants you wish to collect, they are the gatekeeper. Thus, you need to declare the gatekeeper and then provide the evidence of approval.

2-3-Risk
Please refer back to the BPS Ethical Principles to guide how you will minimise risks within your study. You can access the full BPS Code of ethics and conduct on the BPS website.
Nonetheless, the primary ethical principles include:

Respect – valuing the dignity, rights, and autonomy of all participants.
Competence – working within your abilities and seeking supervision where necessary.
Responsibility – ensuring participant welfare, avoiding harm, and managing risk appropriately.
Integrity – conducting research honestly, transparently, and without deception unless ethically justified.

title: Guide to Online Ethics Applications (Wrexham Research Information System (WRIS) / Vidatum Academic)
text:
2-4-Method

Interviews - 1-to-1 interviews between the participant (interviewee) and yourself (the interviewer)
Focus Groups - thematic discussions between participants.
Survey / Questionnaire - Psychometric questionnaires
Observation - Observation to obtain inter-rater scoring.
Non-Invasive experiment - Most psychological / cognitive experiments would be considered as this.
Invasive experiment - This can suggest several things. The one that can be attributed mostly for this high-stress psychological experiments or invasive electrode placements.
Secondary Analysis - You should only do secondary analysis if you are doing a quantitative analysis of the data, such as meta-analysis or a meta synthesis. Therefore this excludes systematic reviews or analyses of previous qualitative research.
Human Tissue – Collecting, storing, or analysing biological samples (e.g., blood, saliva, DNA) to investigate physiological, genetic, or health-related research questions.
Audits / Service Evaluations taking place in the NHS – Assessing existing healthcare services or practices to determine effectiveness, quality, or compliance with standards, rather than generating new generalisable research knowledge.
Internet-mediated research / data mining – Collecting or analysing data gathered through online platforms, social media, forums, digital archives, or large datasets to explore behaviours, attitudes, or trends.
Animals – Conducting research involving live animals to study behaviour, biology, or physiological processes under controlled or observational conditions.
Environmental Methods – Investigating how physical or social environments influence behaviour, wellbeing, or health (e.g., noise, space design, natural vs urban settings).
Visual / Audio Methods – Using images, video, sound recordings, or multimedia materials as primary data sources to analyse behaviour, communication, or experiences.
Auto-ethnography – A reflective research approach where researchers use their own personal experiences as data to explore cultural, social, or psychological phenomena.
Other – Research methods that do not fit into the listed categories and require further explanation or justification within the research proposal.

text:
3-9-Disclosure
To address this question in alignment with BPS guidelines, students must explicitly declare whether their research topic or methods could prompt a participant to disclose risk of harm to self or others, ongoing illegal activity, or safeguarding concerns involving vulnerable populations (Particularly in Qualitative Designs). If such risks exist, students need to demonstrate data minimisation by showing that they are not collecting unnecessary sensitive or identifiable data beyond what is strictly required for the research.
They must then outline a clear escalation protocol detailing how disclosures will be managed—specifically stating that they will immediately inform their academic supervisor to determine if confidentiality must be breached to notify relevant authorities or safeguarding leads. Finally, students must confirm that participants are fully aware of these boundaries before consenting by quoting the exact clause in their Participant Information Sheet and Consent Form that explicitly defines the legal and ethical limits of confidentiality.
Essentially, this comprises of



Requirement
What to write in the application box

Data Minimisation

text:
4-1-Data Type
You have two sections to fill out here; what the data is and how will the data be collected. Just be as pedantic as possible and try to give as much information out as possible so that the reviewer understand what you are trying to do. Sometimes being vague can be at your disadvantage as then the reviewer will question if there’s any ethical considerations you had left out in your application as data is important. S
Specifically to consider, you must highlight why you are collecting specific demographic data. As the are protected characteristics that must be protected unless past research demands it. Essentially, protected characteristics are personal identity attributes that require extra care in research because misuse or disclosure could cause harm, discrimination, or distress. Therefore, if you are trying to obtain specific demographics then please make sure to reference why it is necessary for your research to obtain these characteristics in alignment to your aims and objectives.
A list of common protected characteristics relevant to psychological research:

Age – Including children, adolescents, and older adults, who may require additional consent or capacity considerations.
Disability – Physical, sensory, cognitive, or mental impairments; includes neurodiversity and mental health conditions.
Gender reassignment – Transgender and gender-diverse identities, including transition history.
Marriage and civil partnership – Relevant when research concerns legal, social, or relational status.
Pregnancy and maternity – Including pregnancy status, postnatal experiences, or fertility-related issues.
Race / ethnicity – Including nationality, skin colour, ethnic or cultural background.
Religion or belief – Religious affiliation, spiritual beliefs, or lack of belief.
Sex – Typically referring to biological sex.
Sexual orientation – Sexual identity, attraction, or behaviour.

Ethics committees should and will often ask:

Is this characteristic essential to the research aims?
Could participants be identified or harmed if data were disclosed?
Are recruitment, consent, and reporting respectful and inclusive?

You must clearly describe how your data will be collected or generated. In most cases, data should be collected using approved platforms such as JISC (for surveys), Gorilla.sc (for experimental tasks), Panopto (for interviews / focus groups). If you are collecting data in person without using a dedicated platform, you must outline a clear and structured procedure to ensure that data are collected consistently, handled securely, and stored appropriately on University One Drive.
If your study involves any paper-based materials, you must specify how these will be managed and securely disposed of, including prompt placement into confidential waste bins once data have been transferred or are no longer required. Careful consideration of these procedures is essential, as face-to-face data collection is subject to closer ethical scrutiny, particularly in relation to how participant data are handled, stored, and protected.

text:
4-2-Data Storage
Wrexham University recommends that all research data should be stored on the University server or your university Office 365 accounts as a secure protected and backed up service. Any physical data should be stored securely on University site. Further guidance on the safe storage of research data can be found on the UK Data Service Webpages.

text:
4-3-Access
In this section, you must specify who will have access to the data for the duration of the research project. Access should normally be restricted to you as the student researcher and your supervisor. If your project is advanced in nature or may require technical or methodological support, you should also include psychology technicians as authorised data handlers within the application. Limiting access to only those directly involved in the research helps ensure confidentiality, data security, and compliance with ethical and data protection requirements.

title: Guide to Online Ethics Applications (Wrexham Research Information System (WRIS) / Vidatum Academic)
text:

Student research data should be stored until the end of studies or transferred to the supervisor if required to be retained for a longer period. If required for longer, then necessary data to support or validate a research project’s observations, findings or outputs should be retained in an appropriate format and storage facility for at least 10 years

title: Guide to Online Ethics Applications (Wrexham Research Information System (WRIS) / Vidatum Academic)
text:
4-6-Dissemination
In this section, you should explain where and how your findings will be shared. For most undergraduate and postgraduate projects, this will include:

Submission as part of a dissertation, thesis, or assessed coursework
Presentation to academic staff or examiners
Possible inclusion in poster presentations, internal conferences, or teaching materials

If there is any intention to share findings more widely (e.g. conferences, journal articles, public reports), this should be stated clearly. You should also indicate that results will be reported in an aggregated and anonymised form, rather than at an individual participant level.
Students are not expected to publish their work, but they should be clear and realistic about potential academic dissemination routes. If you seek to publish your work then please speak to your supervisor.
Something to note however, you should demonstrate awareness of how dissemination could affect participants or groups represented in the data. Key ethical considerations typically include:

Anonymity and confidentiality – ensuring that no individual participant can be identified in written reports, presentations, or figures.
Sensitive or protected characteristics – taking care not to stigmatise, stereotype, or misrepresent individuals or groups, particularly where protected characteristics are involved.
Responsible reporting – avoiding sensationalised language, overgeneralisation, or causal claims that are not supported by the data.
Data minimisation – reporting only what is necessary to address the research questions.
Participant dignity – ensuring findings are presented respectfully, even when results are unexpected or negative.

If findings could be misinterpreted or cause distress, students should note how they will contextualise and explain results carefully. In the end, you need to show your understanding who will see your results, how they will be shared, and how you will protect participants from harm or identification when doing so.

title: Guide to Online Ethics Applications (Wrexham Research Information System (WRIS) / Vidatum Academic)
text:
4-7-Storage
Your data should be fully anonymised form as this is best practice to protect your participants. Specifically, this is when the information does not relate to an identified or identifiable person or to personal data rendered anonymous in such a manner that the data subject is not or no longer identifiable.
Please avoid going for identifiable information as this will tagged as high risk and the wait time for your application will extend from 2 weeks.

title: Guide to Online Ethics Applications (Wrexham Research Information System (WRIS) / Vidatum Academic)
text:
4-8-Data Processing
The anonymisation process should be applied as early as possible and maintained throughout the research lifecycle. Nevertheless, this will vary if you are using specific platforms or methodological approaches. Therefore, I have highlighted the following steps as good practice:
Removal of direct identifiers - All direct identifiers (e.g. names, email addresses, student numbers, IP addresses, or usernames) must be removed from the dataset immediately after data collection.
Use of participant codes - Each participant should be assigned a unique, non-identifiable code (e.g. P001, P002). Any document linking participant identities to codes (a “key”) must be stored separately from the research data, in a secure location, and accessed only if absolutely necessary.
Handling of indirect identifiers - Indirect identifiers (e.g. age, gender, ethnicity, job role, or other demographic variables) should be collected only where relevant and reported in aggregated form. Categories may be collapsed where small cell sizes could risk identification.
Anonymisation of qualitative data - For interviews, open-text responses, or observational notes, identifying details (e.g. names of people, places, organisations, or unique events) must be removed or replaced with neutral descriptors (e.g. “[workplace]”, “[friend]”).
Secure storage of anonymised data - Anonymised datasets should be stored on approved, secure systems (e.g.University OneDrive) with restricted access. Identifiable raw data should not be shared or transferred unnecessarily.
Reporting and dissemination - Findings must be reported in a way that prevents identification of individuals or small groups, including careful use of quotations, figures, and tables.
Data retention and destruction - Any temporary files containing identifiable information should be securely deleted once anonymisation is complete and no longer required.

title: Counselling Research Ethics Guidance for Students
text:
Counselling in the UK is not governed by a single statutory regulator. Instead, practitioners belong to professional bodies that hold Accredited Registers overseen by the Professional Standards Authority. The two most relevant to Wrexham Counselling students are:

BACP — British Association for Counselling and Psychotherapy: Ethical Framework for the Counselling Professions
NCPS — National Counselling and Psychotherapy Society: Code of Ethics

For research specifically, BACP publishes a dedicated companion document that the Ethical Framework requires members to follow:

Ethical Guidelines for Research in the Counselling Professions (BACP, last updated February 2019)

NCPS embeds its research requirements directly within the Code of Ethics, in the Research Ethics section.






ImportantThe BACP Ethical Framework is changing



BACP launched a new Ethical Framework for the Counselling Professions 2026, which becomes mandatory at midday on Tuesday 3 November 2026. Until then, the 2018 framework remains the operative document.
The 2026 framework restructures into three sections — working ethically within relationships, ethical principles, and core responsibilities — and adds new guidance on the use of AI and digital technology. It also asks members to articulate a rationale for their ethical decision-making, which is directly relevant to how you justify design choices in an ethics application.
If you are writing a dissertation that will be submitted after November 2026, cite the 2026 framework. If your project concludes before then, cite 2018. Check with your supervisor which applies to your submission date.


A note on which body applies to you. If you are a student member of BACP or NCPS, you are bound by that body’s code now, as a student, not only after qualifying. If you are a member of neither, your project is still governed by Wrexham’s REC and by whichever framework your programme aligns to. Ask your supervisor if you are unsure — the answer changes what you cite in your application.

title: Counselling Research Ethics Guidance for Students
text:
Both frameworks share a common ancestry in principle-based ethics, so they overlap substantially. Where they differ is in emphasis and structure: BACP separates values, principles and personal moral qualities, while NCPS sets out five fundamental principles drawing explicitly on Kitchener (1984) and Kitchener and Anderson (2011).


The 2018 Ethical Framework has three main parts: Our commitment to clients, Ethics, and Good practice. The Ethics section is the one you will most often cite in a research rationale.
BACP core principles:







Principle
Meaning




Being trustworthy
Honouring the trust placed in the practitioner


Autonomy
Respect for the client’s right to be self-governing


Beneficence
A commitment to promoting the client’s wellbeing


Non-maleficence
A commitment to avoiding harm to the client


Justice
Fair and impartial treatment of all clients; adequate provision of services


Self-respect
Fostering the practitioner’s self-knowledge, integrity and care for self



BACP is explicit that these principles will sometimes conflict, and that a decision is not unethical merely because it is controversial or because another practitioner would have decided differently. What is required is that you consider all relevant circumstances with care and remain accountable for the decision you made. This is precisely the reasoning an REC wants to see in an application — not a claim that your study is risk-free, but a demonstration that you identified the tensions and reasoned through them.
BACP also names personal moral qualities that practitioners aspire to, several of which bear directly on research conduct: candour, courage, diligence, humility, integrity, resilience and wisdom.




Working towards the good of clients and doing no harm (Beneficence and Non-maleficence) — practitioners hold client welfare central and commit to avoiding harm.
Being trustworthy and responsible (Fidelity) — honouring trust placed by clients and the community, and representing the profession respectfully.
Respect for the dignity and rights of the client (Autonomy) — the right to self-determination, with Gillick competence and the Fraser Guidelines considered where applicable.
Justice — awareness of one’s own judgements and prejudices, using supervision as a safeguard, and respect for diversity of persons.
Integrity and self-responsibility — honesty and accuracy, alongside responsibility for one’s own health, wellbeing and scope of competence.

NCPS states that these principles cannot deliver a single “right” answer, but can be used to reach a best clinical judgement — and that a practitioner must be able to demonstrate they considered them, especially in discussion with their supervisor.

Self-respect
Principle 5



If your project sits under one body, cite that body. If your cohort spans both, citing the shared principle and noting both sources is acceptable and often clearer.
Do / Do Not Guidance:

✅ Cite the framework your professional membership actually binds you to
✅ Show your reasoning where principles pull against each other
❌ Cite the BPS Code of Human Research Ethics as your governing framework — it governs psychologists, not counsellors
❌ Treat the principles as a checklist to be ticked rather than a reasoning structure

title: Counselling Research Ethics Guidance for Students
text:
The Ethical Framework sets out research obligations in its Good practice section. In summary, BACP members undertaking research commit to being rigorously attentive to the quality and integrity of the research process, the knowledge claims arising from it, and how results are disseminated. All research must be guided by the Ethical Guidelines for Research in the Counselling Professions, all participants must take part on the basis of explicit informed consent, and all research must be reviewed in advance so that participants’ rights and interests are considered independently of the researcher. Research methods must comply with good practice standards for any services being delivered and must not adversely affect clients.
That independent-review requirement is why REC approval is not a bureaucratic formality — it is the mechanism by which the framework’s own standard is met.
The Ethical Guidelines for Research are organised into twelve sections, several of which are directly relevant to dissertation projects:

Ethical principles and research
Research integrity
Safety and managing the risks of research to participants, the public and the researcher
Relationships and communication with research participants
Vulnerability in research participants
Research ethics review and research governance
Online research
Trainee and student researchers
Ethical problem-solving in research

Section 9 is written for you specifically. Read it before drafting your application.



The NCPS Code of Ethics contains a Research Ethics section stating that where research directly involves clients or trainees, all clauses of the Code apply. In addition, researchers must:

Accept that participation is purely voluntary, with no pressure of any type exerted. Payment must not act as an inducement where the research asks participants to take risks beyond those of everyday life.
Obtain proper consent before commencement, especially with minors or persons with special needs. In longitudinal research, consent may need to be repeated at intervals.
Make clear at the outset that initial consent does not negate the right to withdraw at any stage.
Maintain complete openness and honesty about the purpose and nature of the research.
Consider potential adverse consequences and be ready to signpost to support.
Inform a participant if, during research, they present a condition they seem unaware of — and advise them if continued participation may jeopardise their future wellbeing.
Provide for the ongoing care of participants regarding adverse effects arising within a reasonable period after involvement.
Act on the principle that the privacy and psychological wellbeing of the individual participant is always more important than the research itself.

Point 8 is the one to internalise. It is the sentence to return to whenever a design decision trades participant welfare against data quality.






NoteNote on the incentive clause



NCPS permits payment but forbids it as an inducement to accept risk. A modest thank-you (a prize draw entry, a voucher) is generally acceptable; a payment large enough to make a participant tolerate distress they would otherwise avoid is not. Explain your reasoning in the application rather than simply stating the amount.


Do / Do Not Guidance:

✅ Read BACP’s Ethical Guidelines for Research, section 9, if you are a BACP member
✅ Read the NCPS Code’s Research Ethics section if you are an NCPS member
✅ Plan for after-the-fact support, not just in-the-moment debriefing
❌ Assume the Code applies only to clinical work and not to your dissertation
❌ Set an incentive level without justifying it

title: Counselling Research Ethics Guidance for Students
text:
This section has no equivalent in psychology-oriented ethics guidance, and it is the single most common reason counselling dissertation proposals require substantial revision.
As a counselling student you occupy two roles at once: trainee practitioner and student researcher. These roles carry different obligations, different relationships to the people in front of you, and different kinds of power. Confusing them causes real harm.


You must not recruit your own current clients as research participants. The reasons are cumulative and each would be sufficient on its own:

Consent cannot be freely given. A client depends on you therapeutically. “No” is much harder to say to your counsellor than to a stranger with a clipboard.
The therapeutic frame is compromised. Material disclosed in therapy is disclosed for therapeutic purposes. Repurposing it as data breaches the basis on which it was shared.
Dual relationship. BACP requires that dual or multiple relationships be avoided where the risks of harm to the client outweigh the benefits. Researcher-and-therapist is a textbook example.
Withdrawal becomes unsafe. A participant who withdraws mid-study must be able to continue therapy unaffected — and neither of you can be confident that is true.

Former clients are only marginally less problematic, and any such proposal needs explicit supervisory and REC discussion before it is drafted.



Recruiting other clients from your placement agency is sometimes possible but is never straightforward. It requires:

Gatekeeper permission from the agency, in writing, independent of your own placement relationship
Recruitment that does not run through you as their counsellor or a colleague with therapeutic contact
Clear communication that participation has no bearing whatsoever on the service they receive
A plan for what happens if a participant discloses something about the service, a colleague, or their own risk

Many agencies will decline, and they are entitled to. Build your timeline assuming a “no” is possible, and have an alternative population identified before you submit.



Counselling students are, by training, good at opening people up. That skill becomes an ethical hazard in a research interview, where you have no therapeutic contract, no ongoing relationship, and no mandate to work with what emerges.
The distinction to hold onto: you use counselling skills to conduct a humane interview, but you are not offering therapy. You listen well, you notice distress, you respond with warmth — and then you signpost rather than intervene.
Do / Do Not Guidance:

✅ Use counselling skills to make the interview safe, paced and respectful
✅ Pause, offer a break, or end the interview if a participant becomes distressed
✅ Have a written signposting list ready before the first interview
✅ Take the emotional impact of interviews to research supervision
❌ Follow distressing material deeper because it is producing rich data
❌ Offer interpretations, reframes, or therapeutic homework
❌ Slide into a therapeutic contract mid-interview
❌ Research your own current clients under any framing




Clinical supervision and research supervision are different, and you will likely have both. Clinical supervision addresses your practice with clients; research supervision addresses your project. Material from research participants should go to your research supervisor, within the confidentiality terms your participants agreed to — not into clinical supervision, where participants never consented for it to go.
If a research interview has affected you personally, that is appropriate for clinical supervision or personal therapy, discussed at the level of your own reaction rather than the participant’s disclosures.

title: Counselling Research Ethics Guidance for Students
text:
Do / Do Not Guidance:

✅ Provide clear rationale, methodology, and risk management plans
✅ Demonstrate researcher competence and supervision arrangements
✅ State explicitly how you have separated practitioner and researcher roles
❌ Submit vague or incomplete proposals
❌ Assume feasibility without evidence

Key areas of REC evaluation include:

Feasibility within the academic timeframe
Appropriateness of the sample and recruitment method
Data protection, storage, and UK GDPR compliance
Researcher competence and supervision
Institutional risk and liability
Management of dual roles and power imbalance
Adequacy of distress protocols and signposting
Researcher safety and wellbeing

title: Counselling Research Ethics Guidance for Students
text:
This section is more procedural, so that you have a route from research question to submitted application.



Decide upon your research question
Use the university templates: https://wrexham.ac.uk/research/our-research/research-ethics/how-to-apply--university-templates/
Decide the statistical model that fits the question (correlation, linear regression, multiple regression, ANOVA, Poisson, zero-inflated count models, and so on)
Choose psychometric measures of your constructs of interest:

decide how many items you require
decide whether to use an established or a newly validated measure
confirm licensing and permission in writing

Justify each demographic item you collect in relation to your constructs — collect nothing you cannot justify
Obtain approval to use the JISC platform from the technical team, with supervisor approval

Document order for an online survey:

Participant information sheet — the first document the participant sees (unless you are first asking whether they wish to use Welsh-language versions)
Consent form — meeting BACP or NCPS consent requirements, including the explicit right to withdraw
The measures themselves, in the order you have justified
Debrief — how the data will be used, and signposting to appropriate services should participation have affected their wellbeing





Decide upon your research question
Use the university templates linked above
Decide the statistical model that fits the question (t-tests, regression, ANOVA, and so on)
Select a task or measure that works within an experimental procedure
Justify your demographic items
Decide whether the study is face-to-face or online
Consult the technical team, with supervisor approval, on building and deploying the study
[Face-to-face] Arrange room booking and complete the risk assessment
[Gorilla.sc] Obtain platform approval with supervisor approval; work through the Gorilla tutorials; build materials and the experiment tree; obtain tokens; deploy, and use the resulting link in your recruitment advert




Qualitative work is the dominant tradition in counselling research, and the pathway deserves the same specificity.

Decide upon your research question
Decide the methodology: Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis, thematic analysis, grounded theory, narrative analysis, discourse analysis, ethnography
Decide the method: interview, focus group, observation

Document analysis is a secondary data collection method and does not satisfy the primary data collection requirement of the dissertation

Consider reflexivity from the start, not as an appendix. Your own training, assumptions and therapeutic orientation shape what you hear and how you interpret it. Both frameworks require this kind of self-examination — NCPS names awareness of one’s own judgements under Justice; BACP names humility and self-respect among personal moral qualities. Keep a reflexive journal from the first interview
Plan anonymisation at transcription, not at write-up. Change names, places, employers, and distinctive circumstances as you transcribe
Plan for quotation consent. Verbatim quotes are more identifying than students expect, particularly in small professional communities. State in your information sheet that anonymised quotes may be used
Decide face-to-face or online delivery

Face-to-face:

Book a suitable private room; complete the room and lone-working risk assessment
Arrange times with participants that coincide with the booking
Record audio only, via the approved platform

Online:

Use Microsoft Teams with the approved recording platform (not a personal application install)
Test that audio records correctly before your first real interview — a lost first interview is not recoverable and the participant cannot simply repeat it
Consider the participant’s privacy at their end: are they somewhere they can speak freely?

title: Counselling Research Ethics Guidance for Students
text:
Confidentiality in research differs from confidentiality in therapy, and participants need to understand which one applies.
Both frameworks require that limits to confidentiality be stated in advance. In a research context this means your information sheet must say, before consent is given, what would cause you to break confidentiality — typically disclosure of risk of serious harm to the participant or another person, or of a child at risk.
Do / Do Not Guidance:

✅ State the limits of confidentiality before consent, not after a disclosure
✅ Keep records adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary
✅ Store data on institutional systems, encrypted, with access limited to the research team
✅ Agree a retention and destruction schedule and state it to participants
✅ Transport any physical materials in a locked container
❌ Keep recordings on a phone or personal laptop
❌ Promise absolute confidentiality — you cannot deliver it
❌ Discuss identifiable participant material in open forums or group chats
